passage: In the hospital billing office, Divyansh, the supervisor, watched the week unfold. Anand reconciled forty claims by Wednesday and stayed late on Thursday. Priya at the next desk printed the same three forms and spent long stretches at the tea counter. Nobody had complained. Divyansh noticed Anand's shoulders sagging and Priya's empty in-tray. He weighed it up: if he ignored it, Priya would keep coasting, and Anand would burn out. On Friday he asked Priya for a private word: "I want to understand your workload. Can we look at it together?" Then he took Anand aside and said, "I see how much you have done. Let me rebalance."

qa.q: How many claims did Anand reconcile by Wednesday?
qa.a: Anand reconciled forty claims by Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Divyansh worried about when weighing up what to do?
qa.a: Divyansh was concerned that ignoring the imbalance would reward coasting and burn out Anand; the worry was for fairness and for Anand's health.

qa.q: What did Divyansh do on Friday that a fair manager would do?
qa.a: Divyansh spoke privately with each person, asked Priya about the workload without accusing, and told Anand the effort was seen and would be rebalanced.

qa.q: What might Anand have felt when Divyansh said "I see how much you have done"?
qa.a: Anand probably felt relief and a little pride at being noticed after quietly carrying the load; sagging shoulders suggest that being unseen had been wearing.

grounding: A manager sees one person doing heavy lifting and another barely contributing, and chooses a fair, private conversation over ignoring it.

passage: Dear Francis, I need an outside view. On my team of six, Rahul carries about half the work and Tessa produces about a fifth. I can see it every week in the tracker. Rahul never complains and Tessa always smiles in meetings. I have said nothing for two months, and last week Rahul stayed until nine and looked exhausted. I kept telling myself it would even out. It will not. Next week I will speak privately with each of them, first Tessa, to understand what is going on, then Rahul, to thank him and ask what he needs. Tell me if you think I am being unfair to either. — Zainab

qa.q: How long has Zainab said nothing about the uneven work?
qa.a: Zainab has said nothing for two months.

qa.q: What is Zainab feeling as writing that "it will not" even out?
qa.a: Zainab feels uneasy and a bit guilty for waiting so long, and resolved that ignoring the imbalance is not working.

qa.q: What plan does Zainab make about how to raise the issue?
qa.a: Zainab plans private conversations, first with Tessa to understand what is going on, then with Rahul to thank him and ask what he needs.

qa.q: What might Rahul be feeling after staying until nine while never complaining?
qa.a: Rahul probably feels exhausted and perhaps unnoticed, and may also worry that complaining would look bad; the tiredness shows in staying late.

grounding: A manager sees one person doing heavy lifting and another barely contributing, and plans a fair, private conversation.

passage:
So you asked what surprised me about managing? I'm Siddharth, and it was noticing who carried whom.
On my first project as a manager, Maria stayed late every night. Rohit left at five sharp and his updates were always “in progress”. When I checked the files, Maria had done nearly all the design, and even fixed Rohit's parts.
My first instinct was to say nothing. The project was on time. Why rock the boat?
But then I saw Maria rubbing her eyes at a nine a.m. meeting and snapping at an intern. I thought, if I ignore this, I lose her.
So I spoke to Rohit alone first, calmly, with the files open. Then I spoke to Maria. We split the next phase with names on each task.

qa.q: What time did Rohit leave every day?
qa.a: He left at five sharp.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when he saw Maria rubbing her eyes?
qa.a: Siddharth felt worried and uneasy, realising that ignoring the imbalance could burn Maria out.

qa.q: Why was talking to Rohit alone, with the files open, a fair approach?
qa.a: It was private and based on facts, so Rohit could respond without public shame, and it stopped rewarding his coasting.

qa.q: How might Maria have felt before Siddharth spoke to her?
qa.a: She was probably exhausted and resentful, snapping at an intern after carrying Rohit's work.

grounding: A young manager recalls noticing one person doing the heavy lifting and another coasting, and choosing fair private conversations.

passage:
I sit across from Tejas, our team lead, so I saw how it played out, though I can only guess what went on in his head.
For weeks Sharmila did the client calls, the reports and the invoices. Gaurav mostly forwarded emails. The rest of us noticed, of course. We didn't say anything.
Then one Tuesday I saw Tejas looking at the task board for a long time, frowning. He looked at Sharmila, who was eating lunch at her desk again, then at Gaurav, who was out for his third tea.
That afternoon he took Gaurav into the small room. The door was closed for twenty minutes. The next day he did the same with Sharmila.
By Friday, Gaurav had his own client calls. Sharmila went home at six.

qa.q: Where was Sharmila eating lunch?
qa.a: She was eating lunch at her desk again.

qa.q: What did Tejas's long frown at the task board suggest?
qa.a: It suggested he felt concerned and troubled by the uneven effort, noticing that Sharmila was overloaded.

qa.q: What did Tejas do that worked?
qa.a: He spoke to Gaurav and Sharmila privately, one at a time, and then shared the work more fairly.

qa.q: How might Sharmila have felt going home at six on Friday?
qa.a: She likely felt relieved and valued, finally not carrying Gaurav's share.

grounding: A colleague describes a team lead noticing uneven effort and holding fair, private conversations instead of ignoring it.

passage:
Week one: Kavitha, newly promoted to manage the bakery's night shift, noticed that Naveen was always kneading dough when she arrived. Arjun and Suresh were on their phones in the back.
Week two: She checked the prep sheets. Naveen had done most of the bread, the cakes and the cleaning. Arjun's name was on sheets he hadn't touched. Naveen's hands shook when he lifted the heavy trays. Kavitha felt a knot in her stomach. If she did nothing, she'd lose her best baker.
Week three: She spoke to Arjun and Suresh one by one in the storeroom, calmly, with the prep sheets. Then she thanked Naveen privately and made a new rota with names on each task. Arjun grumbled but showed up on time.

qa.q: Where did Kavitha speak to Arjun and Suresh?
qa.a: She spoke to them in the storeroom.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha feel a knot in her stomach in week two?
qa.a: She felt worried and uneasy, fearing that if she ignored the imbalance she would lose her best baker.

qa.q: What steps did Kavitha take, and why were they fair?
qa.a: She talked privately with each loafer using the prep sheets as evidence, thanked Naveen and made a named rota, fixing it without public shaming.

qa.q: How might Naveen have felt when Kavitha thanked him privately?
qa.a: He probably felt seen and relieved after weeks of doing others' work, maybe a little emotional.

grounding: Shows a young manager noticing one worker doing heavy lifting while others coast, and holding fair private talks to fix it.

passage:
Jaya, you asked how old Jomon handles a team where one person does everything. Let me tell you about my first team, at a printing press in Kochi.
I was twenty-five, managing four people. Susan did the proofs, the layouts, the late-night fixes. Benny chatted with clients and somehow never had a finished page. For months I said nothing. Susan never complained, and Benny made everyone laugh.
Then one evening I found Susan asleep on the paper stacks at nine, and Benny's desk empty since four. That's when I saw it: by keeping quiet, I was paying for Benny's ease with Susan's health.
Next morning I took Benny out for tea, just the two of us. No shouting. I showed him the job sheet and asked, "What's getting in your way?" He went red, then admitted he was scared of the new layout software. Within a month he was doing his share, and Susan finally took her leave.

qa.q: Where was Jomon's first team?
qa.a: At a printing press in Kochi.

qa.q: What did young Jomon feel on finding Susan asleep on the paper stacks?
qa.a: Jomon felt a jolt of guilt and alarm, realising that months of silence had been costing Susan her health.

qa.q: Which choice in the story turned things around, and why?
qa.a: Talking to Benny privately over tea with the job sheet and a real question; it uncovered the fear of the software without shaming him.

qa.q: What might Benny have felt when shown the job sheet?
qa.a: Benny was embarrassed, since he went red, but perhaps relieved to finally admit being scared of the software.

grounding: Shows a young manager who notices one person carrying the load while another coasts, and resolves it through a fair, private conversation.
